chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Kalman Filter for Dynamic Hedge Ratios

lessons.title: Case Study: Static vs Kalman Filter Hedge Ratio on the Same NSE Pair

children.text: Lessons 17 to 19 built the argument and the mechanism. This lesson shows the actual payoff: running a static hedge ratio and a Kalman-tracked hedge ratio side by side, on the exact same month of HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank prices, and watching how differently they behave. (All prices and statistical output in this case study are illustrative.)

body.text: A static hedge ratio and a Kalman-tracked hedge ratio can start out identical and diverge sharply within weeks if the true relationship drifts, one producing a false trading signal, the other correctly staying calm, using the exact same underlying prices.

children.text: The Setup: One Month, Two Hedge Ratios

Picking up where Lesson 6 left off, ICICI Bank at ₹1,000 and HDFC Bank at ₹1,599, imagine the pair's real relationship drifts smoothly over the following month, echoing the kind of structural shift Lesson 17 described, from β ≈ 1.39 up to β ≈ 1.58 by month's end. Here is what the two stocks' prices look like at five weekly checkpoints.

body.caption: One month of prices, with the pair's true (but not directly observable) beta drifting (illustrative)

children.text: Two Spreads, Same Prices, Different Beta

The static spread uses Lesson 6's original β ≈ 1.39 for every single week, unchanged. The Kalman spread uses the filter's own tracked estimate, which lags the true drift slightly, exactly as a real filter would, but keeps closing the gap: 1.390, 1.421, 1.468, 1.514, 1.556 across the five weeks. Both spreads use the same intercept from Lesson 6, so the comparison isolates exactly the effect a drifting β has on its own.

body.text: A trader using the static hedge ratio sees a z-score of +2.05 at Week 5 and, following Lesson 14's rule exactly as written, would enter a trade betting on reversion. But there is nothing to revert. The Kalman-tracked view shows the pair's real, current relationship is close to normal. The static spread only looks stretched because it is comparing today's prices against a β that stopped being accurate weeks earlier.

children.text: Why This Matters More Than It Might Seem

This is a different failure mode from the structural breaks Lessons 4, 8, and 11 discussed. In those cases, the pair's actual relationship had genuinely changed or was in doubt. Here, the pair's real relationship was fine the entire time, it simply moved gradually, the way relationships do. The failure was entirely in the measurement: a hedge ratio that stopped being updated. In some ways this is more dangerous than an obvious structural break, because nothing about the pair itself looks broken, only the number a trader forgot to keep current.

body.title: Would this static-hedge-ratio trade actually work?
body.scenario: Using the static β = 1.39 hedge ratio, a trader sees the Week 5 z-score of +2.05 and, following Lesson 14's rule, shorts the spread: short HDFC Bank, long ICICI Bank in the old 1.39 ratio, betting on reversion.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson's numbers, is this trade likely to behave the way the trader expects, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Almost certainly not, at least not for the reason the trader thinks. The Kalman-tracked view shows the pair's actual current relationship is close to normal (z ≈ +0.90); nothing is genuinely stretched. The static spread only looks extreme because it is comparing today's prices against an outdated β from weeks earlier. There is no real mean-reversion opportunity here to capture, and the trader is also sizing the position with the stale 1.39 ratio, which is not even properly hedged against the pair's real current sensitivity, compounding the problem.

body.title: What is actually different between the two spreads?
body.question: In this case study, both the static and Kalman spreads use the exact same underlying HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank prices. What explains the very different-looking results?
options: The Kalman spread used different, more recent price data
Only the β used to compute the predicted HDFC price differs between the two: static holds it fixed at 1.39, Kalman lets it track the pair's real, evolving relationship
The static spread contains a calculation error
Z-scores cannot be computed on a spread built with a Kalman-filtered hedge ratio
body.explanation: Both spreads are computed from identical prices. The only difference is which β is used to build the predicted HDFC price at each point: a single frozen number for the static version, versus the Kalman filter's continuously updated estimate. That one difference is entirely responsible for one spread trending steadily upward and the other staying bounded.

cards.definition: A misleading entry or exit signal produced not because a pair's real relationship has broken down, but because the hedge ratio used to compute its spread and z-score is outdated.
A spread that stays within a roughly stable range over time, the visual signature of a hedge ratio that is still correctly tracking the pair's real relationship.

points: Using the exact same HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank prices, a static β = 1.39 hedge ratio produced a spread that grew steadily from ₹1 to ₹225 across one illustrative month, while a Kalman-tracked β produced a spread that stayed roughly bounded between ₹1 and ₹26.

At the final checkpoint, the static hedge ratio's z-score reached +2.05, past Lesson 14's entry threshold, a signal to trade. The Kalman-tracked z-score sat at a calm +0.90, correctly showing nothing unusual once the pair's real, current relationship is accounted for.

This is a distinct failure mode from a genuine structural break (Lessons 4, 8, and 11): the pair's real relationship here was fine throughout. It was the measurement, the static hedge ratio, that had gone stale.
A trade entered on the static spread's false signal would not be exploiting genuine mean reversion, and would also be improperly hedged, using a β that no longer matches the pair's real sensitivity.
This closes Chapter 5's case for dynamic hedge ratios: the Kalman filter isn't just a smoother way to estimate β, it can materially change which trading signals a strategy would have acted on.
